summary: This Best Current Practice document compiles the process for selecting, confirming, and recalling members of the IAB and IESG, and some members of the IAOC, through nominating and recall committees. It was replaced by RFC 8713.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7437 explains how the IETF picks the people who run its working groups and steer its standards process. A committee chosen at random reviews the empty positions and puts forward candidates, and a separate body approves them. The document also says how a member can be asked to step down.

subtitle: How the IETF chooses, confirms and can recall the people who run its working groups.

tldr.problem: The IETF's steering groups and advisory board need people in them, and those people have to be chosen in a way the community accepts. The choice also has to be hard to rig, and there has to be a way to remove someone who is not doing the job.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7437 describes a nominating committee that is picked at random from volunteers, reviews the open positions, and nominates candidates. A separate confirming body then approves or rejects each candidate, and the confirming body is the IAB for IESG candidates, the Internet Society Board of Trustees for IAB candidates, and the IAOC for the IAOC candidate.
tldr.outcome: The document also sets out how a dispute is resolved and how a recall petition works, where a committee of volunteers investigates and a three-quarter majority of those who vote is needed to remove a sitting member. It replaced RFC 3777 and was later obsoleted by RFC 8713.

today: RFC 7437 is a Best Current Practice that consolidated RFC 3777 and the documents that had updated it into a single specification. It was itself updated by RFC 8318 and obsoleted by RFC 8713.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
This document is a revision of and supersedes BCP 10. In essence it republishes RFC 3777 and the other RFCs that updated that document into a single specification, giving a complete description of the process by which members of the IAB and IESG, and some members of the IAOC, are selected, confirmed and recalled as of the date of its approval. Section 4 of RFC 4071 gives further details about the IAOC positions filled by the nominating committee.

Two assumptions continue to hold. The IRTF and its steering group are not part of the process described here, and neither is the organisation or reorganisation of the IESG.

The time frames use IETF meetings as a frame of reference and assume that the IETF meets three times per calendar year with roughly equal time between meetings. Those meetings are called the First, Second and Third IETF as needed.

The document is divided into four topics. The first is the general set of rules and constraints that apply to the selection and confirmation process as a whole. The second is the process by which the volunteers who serve on the nominating committee are selected. The third is the set of principles, rules and constraints that guide the committee's activities, including the confirmation process. The fourth is the process by which the behaviour of a sitting member of the IAOC, IESG or IAB may be questioned, perhaps resulting in the removal of that member. An appendix collects useful facts and practices from previous nominating committees, and another sets out how the document differs from its predecessor.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is one long rulebook for a yearly ritual: choosing volunteers, having them pick candidates, and having another body say yes or no. It also says what happens when somebody in one of these roles is doing a bad job.

sections.title: General Rules for the Annual Process
sections.content:
The completion of the annual process is due within seven months, one month before the Friday of the week before the First IETF, and it is expected to begin at least eight months before that Friday. The process officially begins when the Chair of the committee is announced and ends when all confirmed candidates have been announced. It has three components: selecting and organising the nominating committee members, selecting the candidates, and confirming the candidates. An extra month is set aside between the end of the process and the start of the new candidates' terms, and may be used to extend any of the components.

The principal functions of the nominating committee are to review each open IESG, IAB and IAOC position and to nominate either its incumbent or a superior candidate. The committee does not choose which positions to review; it is told, together with a brief summary of the expertise wanted for each one. Incumbents must notify the committee if they wish to be nominated. The committee does not confirm its own candidates; it presents them to the confirming body.

Approximately one half of the then current IESG and IAB positions, and one IAOC position, are selected for review each year, so that roughly half of each body's members is reviewed annually. Confirmed candidates are expected to serve at least a two-year term, and the committee may assign a term of not more than three years to one or more positions so that the half-and-half pattern still works.

Mid-term vacancies are filled under the same rules with four qualifications. The confirming body has two weeks from being notified of a candidate to reject it, or the candidate is assumed confirmed. The term of a confirmed candidate is either the remainder of the open position's term if that remainder is at least a year, or the remainder plus the next two-year term if it is less than a year. If the committee is reconvened to fill a mid-term vacancy, the selection and confirmation is due within six weeks.

All deliberations and supporting information about specific nominees, candidates and confirmed candidates are confidential. The list of nominees willing to be considered is not confidential, and the committee may disclose it to gather community feedback, though nominees should not encourage public statements of support.

Unless otherwise specified, an advice and consent model is used. The committee selects candidates based on its understanding of the community's consensus about the qualifications required, and advises each confirming body of its candidates. The confirming bodies review the candidates and consent to some, all or none. The sitting IAB members review the IESG candidates, the Internet Society Board of Trustees reviews the IAB candidates, and the IAOC candidate is reviewed as specified in RFC 4071. A confirming body with no rule of its own should need at least one half of its sitting members to agree to confirm a candidate.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole thing runs on a yearly clock tied to the three IETF meetings. Each year about half of the IESG and IAB seats are up for review, and a committee of volunteers proposes people for them. The proposals then go to a separate body, which can approve some, all or none of them.

sections.title: Choosing and Organising the Committee
sections.content:
The nominating committee comprises at least a Chair, 10 voting volunteers, two liaisons and an advisor. The Chair is appointed by the Internet Society President and must meet the same requirements as a voting volunteer, and the appointment is due no later than the Second IETF meeting so that it can be announced at that meeting. The Chair must be thoroughly familiar with the rules in the document, must ensure the committee completes its duties consistently with it, and must attest at a plenary session of the First IETF that the results represent the committee's best effort and the best interests of the IETF community. The Chair does not vote on the selection of candidates.

The liaisons are appointed by the sitting IAB and IESG members from their own current membership, and must not be sitting in an open position. They are expected to represent their organisations, to answer questions from the committee, and to report concerns about the committee's operation immediately. The Internet Society Board of Trustees may appoint a liaison of its own. The Chair of the prior year's nominating committee serves as an advisor.

To become a voting volunteer, a person must have attended at least three of the last five IETF meetings, and must supply a full name, an email address and a primary company or organisation affiliation. Anyone serving on the Internet Society Board of Trustees, the IAB, the IESG or the IAOC, including in an ex officio position, may not volunteer as a voting member. The solicitation must give the community at least 30 days to volunteer.

The Chair announces the pool of volunteers and the method used to select from it, at least one week before the selection takes place. The method must depend on random data whose value is not known until the day, it must be independently verifiable as fair and unbiased, and it must be repeatable so that unavailable volunteers can be replaced. The Chair then selects the 10 voting volunteers at random. No more than two volunteers with the same primary affiliation may be selected, and a volunteer who duplicates an affiliation already selected is removed and the method repeated.

There must be at least two announcements of the members. After the first, the community has at least one week to challenge the result in writing, and the Chair has 48 hours to review a challenge and propose a resolution. Once 10 voting volunteers are confirmed as willing and available, the Chair makes the second announcement, which officially begins the committee's term. The committee then has about one month to organise itself, setting up a teleconference schedule, an internal web site, a mailing list, an email address for community input, operational procedures and milestones.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee is picked at random from volunteers who have been to enough meetings, so that nobody can stack it with friends. The method has to be public and repeatable, and anyone can challenge the result for a week. No more than two people from the same employer may end up on it.

sections.title: Running the Committee and Selecting Candidates
sections.content:
The Chair must establish a voting mechanism and a set of milestones for selecting candidates and confirming them. Only the voting volunteers vote on a candidate selection, and for such a vote a quorum is at least seven of them. At all other times a quorum is present if at least 75 percent of the nominating committee members are participating.

Any committee member may propose that another member, except the Chair, be recalled. A member may be recalled if at least a quorum of all committee members agree, including the vote of the member being recalled. Only the prior year's Chair may request the recall of the current Chair. If a single voting volunteer position is vacated, the committee may proceed with nine voting volunteers at its own discretion; in all other cases a new voting member must be selected and the random selection repeated.

Any member of the IETF community may nominate any other member for any open position, and a self-nomination is permitted. Nominating committee members are not eligible to be considered for open positions while they serve, though they may be nominated by the following committee. Members who were recalled from any IESG, IAB or IAOC position during the previous two years are not eligible. Nominees must consent in writing to their nomination, with a commitment to provide the resources needed for the position.

The committee then selects candidates based on its understanding of the community's consensus about the qualifications required, consulting a broad base of the IETF community. It advises the confirming bodies of its candidates, specifying a single candidate for each open position and testifying as to how that candidate meets the qualifications of the position. Confirmed candidates must consent to their confirmation, and rejected nominees and candidates must be notified before the confirmed candidates are announced. The committee should archive the information it collects for no longer than its term, so that it could fill a mid-term vacancy if it had to.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the committee is in place it asks the community who should fill the open seats, argues about it in private, and then passes its picks on to the body that has to approve them. Anything said about a specific person stays inside the committee.

sections.title: Dispute Resolution and Recall
sections.content:
The nominating committee operates under a strict rule of confidentiality, so when process issues arise it is best to resolve them within the committee. When that is not possible, a dispute resolution process applies. Its results are final and binding, with no appeal. The process begins with a written request to the Internet Society President, who appoints an arbiter to investigate. The arbiter makes every reasonable effort to understand both sides, decides on a resolution after consulting the two principal parties, summarises the issue and the rationale for the President, and prepares a report that does not violate the committee's confidentiality. The Chair includes the dispute report when reporting to the community. While the dispute is open, the committee may continue activities unrelated to it but must not submit candidates to a confirming body. The process should be completed within two weeks.

Separately, a sitting member can be asked to step down. At any time, at least 20 members of the IETF community who are qualified to be voting members of a nominating committee may request the recall of any sitting IAB, IAOC or IESG member by signed petition to the Internet Society President. The same affiliation limit applies, so no more than two signatories may share a primary affiliation. The petition must include a justification and supporting documentation, and it and its signatories must be announced to the community.

The Internet Society President appoints a Recall Committee Chair and must not evaluate the recall request, because it is explicitly the responsibility of the IETF community to evaluate the behaviour of its leaders. The recall committee is created by the same rules as the nominating committee, with the qualification that neither the member being investigated nor the parties requesting the recall may be on it in any capacity, and it operates by the same rules except that there is no confirmation process. It investigates the circumstances and votes on its findings, and the investigation must include an opportunity for the member to present a written statement and consultation with third parties. A three-quarter majority of the members who vote is required for a recall. If a sitting member is recalled, the open position is filled under the mid-term vacancy rules.
sections.plainLanguage: If the committee cannot settle a problem itself, the Internet Society President appoints someone to settle it, and that decision cannot be appealed. Removing a serving member is even harder: twenty qualified community members must sign a petition, a fresh committee investigates, and three quarters of those who vote must agree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Any selection, confirmation or recall process necessarily involves investigation into the qualifications and activities of prospective candidates, and the investigation may reveal confidential or otherwise private information about them. Each person who participates in any aspect of the process must maintain the confidentiality of any information not explicitly identified as suitable for public dissemination. When the nominating committee decides it needs to share confidential information with others, the dissemination must be minimal and must include a prior commitment from all those consulted to observe the same confidentiality rules as the committee itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The process involves learning private things about private people. Everyone taking part has to keep that information to themselves, and to make anyone they consult promise the same.

items.label: Quorum for a candidate selection vote

items.label: Quorum at all other times
items.desc: At least 75% of the nominating committee members must be participating.

items.label: Default confirmation rule
items.desc: Confirming a candidate should need at least one half of the confirming body's sitting members.

items.label: Signatories for a recall petition
items.desc: At least 20 qualified members of the IETF community.

items.label: Recall majority
items.desc: A three-quarter majority of the members who vote is required.
